"With a record of working across the aisle to develop sound bipartisan legislation, he would offer a choice to a broader range of Americans than the rest of the Republican field." The endorsement anticipated readers asking how the New York paper could reject Giuliani, a man it endorsed for re-election in 1997 and praised for his work cleaning up crime in the city and during the time of the September 11, 2001 attacks. "That man is not running for president," the paper wrote. "The Rudolph Giuliani of 2008 first shamelessly turned the horror of 9/11 into a lucrative business, with a secret client list, then exploited his city's and the country's nightmare to promote his presidential campaign," the paper writes, describing Giuliani as "a narrow, obsessively secretive, vindictive man." Giuliani played down the harsh words, suggesting that the Times has a liberal editorial staff that often disapproved of him. "I changed welfare, I changed quality of life, I took on homelessness -- I did all the things that they think makes you mean and I believe show true compassion and true love for people." The editorial was hardly full of praise for McCain, despite calling him a "genuine war hero" and a "staunch advocate of campaign finance reform." "Mr. McCain was one of the first prominent Republicans to point out how badly the war in Iraq was being managed. We wish he could now see as clearly past the temporary victories produced by Mr. Bush's unsustainable escalation, which have not led to any change in Iraq's murderous political calculus," it reads. "At the least, he owes Americans a real idea of how he would win this war, which he says he can do." The paper praised Clinton's chief rival, Sen. Barack Obama, but called Clinton more qualified for the job. "It is unfair, especially after seven years of Mr. Bush's inept leadership, but any Democrat will face tougher questioning about his or her fitness to be commander in chief," it reads. "Mrs. Clinton has more than cleared that bar, using her years in the Senate well to immerse herself in national security issues, and has won the respect of world leaders and many in the American military." The Democratic editorial contrasts Clinton and Obama -- calling her "the brilliant if at times harsh-sounding senator from New York" and him "the incandescent if still undefined senator from Illinois." The paper says Clinton "sometimes overstates the importance of [her] resume," but that upon hearing "her policies and answers for America's big problems, we are hugely impressed by the depth of her knowledge, by the force of her intellect and by the breadth of, yes, her experience." The paper characterized him as "a narrow, obsessively secretive, vindictive man."

Giuliani brushed aside the criticism, implying that the Times employs a liberal editorial team that has frequently opposed him. "I probably never did anything the New York Times suggested I do in eight years as mayor of New York City, and if I did, I wouldn't be considered a conservative Republican," he remarked at a GOP debate held Thursday evening by MSNBC in Boca Raton, Florida. Giuliani's campaign wasn't alone in using this strategy. A message from the team of former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney mockingly pointed out that McCain had received the blessing of "[t]hat bastion of conservative advocacy."

The editorial offered McCain limited praise, even as it described him as a "genuine war hero" and a "staunch advocate of campaign finance reform." It observed that he had been among the earliest high-profile Republicans to highlight the mismanagement of the Iraq war, then expressed hope that he could now recognize that the short-term gains from Bush's unsustainable troop buildup have failed to alter Iraq's deadly political dynamics. The board added that, at minimum, McCain owed the public a genuine plan for achieving the victory he claims is possible.

While the newspaper spoke highly of Clinton's main competitor, Sen. Barack Obama, it deemed Clinton better suited for the presidency. It acknowledged the unfairness -- particularly following seven years of what it called Bush's incompetent leadership -- but noted that any Democrat would encounter more intense scrutiny regarding their qualifications to serve as commander in chief. The paper concluded that Clinton had far exceeded that standard, having spent her Senate tenure deeply engaged in national security matters while earning the esteem of foreign leaders and numerous members of the U.S. military.

In its Democratic endorsement, the Times drew a distinction between the two candidates, describing Clinton as "the brilliant if at times harsh-sounding senator from New York" and Obama as "the incandescent if still undefined senator from Illinois." Although the paper conceded that Clinton "sometimes overstates the importance of [her] resume," it wrote that after reviewing her proposals and solutions for the country's major challenges, the board was profoundly impressed by the depth of her knowledge, the power of her intellect, and the extent of her experience.

The newspaper endorsed Arizona Senator John McCain for the Republican presidential nomination. In its endorsement, the Times highlighted McCain's reputation for reaching across the political aisle, praising his bipartisan record and his willingness to work with members of both parties on key legislative issues. The paper portrayed him as a candidate of principle and experience, distinguishing him from his rivals in the Republican field.

## Democratic Endorsement

On the Democratic side, the Times endorsed Hillary Clinton, then a senator from New York, for her party's nomination. The endorsement reflected the newspaper's confidence in her qualifications and vision for the country.

## Sharp Criticism of Rudy Giuliani

Perhaps most striking was the newspaper's sharp criticism of former New York City mayor Rudy Giuliani—a notable reversal given that the Times had endorsed Giuliani in his 1997 mayoral reelection bid. In its assessment, the paper described Giuliani as a "narrow, obsessively secretive, vindictive man," delivering an unusually harsh characterization of a former local official the paper had once supported.

The editorial went further, accusing Giuliani of exploiting the tragedy of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks for both personal profit and political advantage. This criticism struck at the heart of Giuliani's presidential campaign, which had been built substantially around his leadership in the aftermath of 9/11.

## Giuliani's Response

Giuliani was quick to dismiss the newspaper's criticism. Rather than engaging directly with the specific charges, he pointed to the Times' well-known liberal editorial stance, effectively framing the criticism as the predictable product of a politically opposed publication and thereby attempting to blunt its impact among Republican primary voters.

**Editorial board praises Arizona senator's independence, backs Clinton over Obama in Democratic contest**

The New York Times editorial board announced its endorsements in the 2008 presidential primaries, throwing its support behind Senator John McCain of Arizona for the Republican nomination and Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton of New York for the Democratic nomination.

In its endorsement of McCain, the newspaper praised the senator's record of independence and his willingness to break with his party on key issues. The editorial highlighted McCain's stance against torture, his work on campaign finance reform, and his candor with voters as reasons for the endorsement.

"We have shuddered at Mr. McCain's occasional, tactical retreats from principle," the board wrote, while nonetheless concluding that he remained the strongest choice in a Republican field the paper viewed with considerable skepticism.

## Sharp Criticism for Giuliani

The endorsement reserved some of its most pointed language for former New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, whom the editorial board knows well from his tenure leading the city. The Times delivered a stinging assessment of Giuliani, describing him as "the most dangerous" of the Republican candidates.

The board criticized what it characterized as Giuliani's divisive style and his approach to executive power, drawing on the paper's familiarity with his record during his time as mayor. The harsh critique of a hometown figure drew particular attention given the newspaper's long observation of Giuliani's political career.

## Backing Clinton in Democratic Race

On the Democratic side, the Times chose Clinton over her chief rival, Senator Barack Obama of Illinois, in what the editorial acknowledged was a difficult choice between two historic candidacies.

The board praised Clinton's depth of experience, command of policy detail, and readiness to assume the presidency. While the editorial expressed admiration for Obama's message and appeal, it ultimately concluded that Clinton was better prepared to lead from day one.

"The next president needs to start immediately on challenges that will require concrete solutions, resolve, and the ability to make government work," the board wrote in explaining its preference for the New York senator.

## Campaign Reactions

The endorsements drew responses from the campaigns, with those receiving the paper's backing welcoming the news while rivals downplayed its significance.

Supporters of the endorsed candidates touted the Times' backing as validation of their campaigns' strengths, while campaigns for other candidates noted that newspaper endorsements do not always translate into votes at the ballot box.

The endorsements come as both parties head into a competitive stretch of primary and caucus contests, with the nominations far from settled in either race.

The New York Times, which endorsed Rudolph Giuliani in his 1997 bid for reelection as mayor of New York City, has declined to support his current campaign, marking a notable reversal that the former mayor addressed during a Republican presidential debate in Florida.

# New York Times Editorial Board Endorses Clinton and McCain Ahead of Super Tuesday

**January 25, 2008** — The New York Times editorial board issued its primary endorsements today, backing Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton for the Democratic nomination and Senator John McCain for the Republican nomination, as both parties prepare for the pivotal Super Tuesday contests on February 5.

The dual endorsements, published in separate editorials, offered a window into how the newspaper's editorial board assessed the leading candidates in what has become one of the most closely watched nomination battles in decades.

## The Democratic Endorsement: Clinton Over Obama

In endorsing Clinton, the editorial board emphasized experience and preparedness while acknowledging the historic and inspirational nature of Barack Obama's candidacy. The board framed its choice as one between two exceptionally strong candidates who represented a break from the past.

The Times praised Clinton as the more seasoned and knowledgeable candidate, describing her command of policy detail and her readiness to assume the presidency. The board highlighted what it characterized as her deep understanding of the challenges facing the nation, from health care to foreign policy, and her demonstrated ability to work within the political system to achieve results.

Regarding Obama, the editorial board was notably warm, describing him as a genuinely inspirational figure whose candidacy had energized the electorate and offered a compelling vision of national unity. The board acknowledged the power of his message and his potential. However, the editorial suggested that Obama's relative lack of experience on the national stage made Clinton the safer and more prepared choice at that moment.

The board did not shy away from noting Clinton's vulnerabilities, including concerns about the tenor of her campaign and questions about the role former President Bill Clinton would play. The editorial urged her to run a more elevated campaign and to distance herself from the more divisive tactics that had emerged during the contest.

## The Republican Endorsement: McCain With Reservations

On the Republican side, the board endorsed McCain, praising his independence, his willingness to break with his party, and his stances on issues such as campaign finance reform, immigration, and the treatment of detainees. The editorial commended McCain's personal integrity and his record of what it viewed as principled positions, even when they put him at odds with Republican orthodoxy.

The board contrasted McCain favorably against his Republican rivals, presenting him as the most reasonable and substantive option in the field.

At the same time, the endorsement contained pointed criticism. The board expressed significant disagreement with McCain on major issues, most notably his support for the war in Iraq and his continued backing of the U.S. military presence there. The editorial also criticized shifts in his positions on tax cuts and other matters, suggesting he had at times compromised his independent reputation to court conservative voters.

## Context and Reception

The endorsements came at a critical juncture in both nomination fights. On the Democratic side, Clinton and Obama were locked in an increasingly competitive and occasionally contentious race following early contests in Iowa, New Hampshire, and other states. On the Republican side, McCain had emerged as a frontrunner following key primary victories, positioning himself against rivals including Mitt Romney.

The Times endorsements, while influential within certain segments of the electorate, ultimately did not determine the outcomes. Obama would go on to secure the Democratic nomination after a prolonged primary battle, while McCain successfully captured the Republican nomination before losing the general election to Obama in November 2008.

The contrasting tone of the two endorsements—enthusiastic for Clinton with acknowledgment of Obama's appeal, and supportive of McCain with substantive policy reservations—reflected the editorial board's effort to weigh experience against inspiration among the Democrats and to balance admiration for McCain's character against disagreement with his policies among the Republicans.
